title: One more disk, twice the work
hook: Each extra disk makes the tower puzzle longer. By how much?

knows: moving one thing at a time
the rule that a bigger disk never sits on a smaller one
doesNotKnow: that moving n disks means solving the n-1 disk puzzle twice
powers of two minus one as a pattern

misconception: Each added disk adds a few more moves, so 6 disks need roughly twice the moves of 3.
objective: The learner can explain that moving n disks means moving the top n-1 aside, moving the biggest, and moving n-1 back, so each extra disk doubles the work plus one: 7, 15, 31, 63.

claims.text: To move a tower, everything above the biggest disk must first be moved off it and onto a third peg, the biggest disk moves once, then the rest is moved back on top.
claims.source: The biggest disk can only move when it has nothing on top and the target peg is empty (every other disk is smaller), so all n-1 others must be on the third peg; afterwards they must all come back onto it. Standard argument, e.g. Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics, 2nd ed., 1.1.

claims.text: The fewest moves is 7 for 3 disks, 15 for 4, 31 for 5 and 63 for 6: each extra disk doubles the work and adds one.
claims.source: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1, so T(n) = 2^n - 1 by induction (Concrete Mathematics, 1.1, eq. 1.1-1.3). Builder computed 2^n - 1 for n = 3..6: 7, 15, 31, 63.

claims.text: The stage shortcut moves the top n-1 disks as one block and charges 2^(n-1) - 1 moves, the fewest that smaller puzzle needs; adding a disk shows the sum: the smaller puzzle, the big disk (1), the smaller puzzle again.
claims.source: Demo.tsx carry(): adds cost(n-1) = 2^(n-1) - 1 to the move counter, per claim c2.

recall.question: A Tower of Hanoi with 7 disks needs 127 moves at best. About how many does 8 disks need?
recall.why: Move the top 7 aside (127), the big disk (1), the top 7 back (127): 127 x 2 + 1 = 255. Each disk doubles the work, plus one.
